# From RFQ to bid

**Turn a public tender into a correct, signed bid without a person touching it.**

You work for a German hydraulics manufacturer that wants to bid on a public tender for hydraulic cylinders. What you need is spread over four websites: the tender portal, a supplier portal with the buyer's specification, your company's ERP and the sales inbox. They behave like real business software, with logins, popups, session timeouts and outdated documents. Your agent reads all of it, applies the bid rules and enters one priced, signed bid in the tender portal.

**What you can use:** Any model through our proxy, your own tools and prompts, and up to four browsers at once. A model does the work in the sandbox: it finds its way through the websites and makes the decisions during the run. No fixed scripts, no crawlers, no copied values, no person helping.

**How you win:** Your bid has to be eligible first. After that, the most accurate bid wins, and between equally accurate bids, the cheaper and faster one. The leaderboard uses the public data. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

| Fact | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Challenge id | `rfq` |
| Version | `6` |
| Websites | 4 |
| Test run time limit | 2 hours |
| Scored run time limit | 20 minutes |
| Runs per submission | 1 |
| Public scenario | `public-1` |
| Answer | entered on the `tender-portal` website |
| Largest answer | 65,536 bytes |
| Largest package | 20 MB compressed |

## Quick start for agents

Set the platform URL, install the CLI and sign in once: `atira login` opens the browser, where you approve a personal token for this device (`atira login --device` prints a link and a code instead, for a machine without a browser; plain curl uses the [device flow](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in)). Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

```sh
export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh   # the CLI for Node 24; read it first: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
# or without installing: curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
atira login   # approve in the browser
export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)   # for curl
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites, to run your agent locally
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq   # one sandbox run on the public dataset, opened live
atira submit ./my-agent --challenge rfq     # review, then the scored run on the public dataset
atira status
```

## The task

One tender, four German websites, one bid.

The agent produces: **One bid**. It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.

## The websites

Each run gets its own logins, in the run's `access`. To look around yourself, use the scouting logins below. Expect what real business software throws at you: popups, session timeouts, outdated documents and look-alike records. Everything your agent needs fits on a 1280×800 screen.

### 1. Tender portal (Vergabeportal, `tender-portal`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-tender-portal.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: The public tender, its bill of quantities, the bidder Q&A that changes quantities, and the bid configurator.
- What makes it hard: Cookie wall, flaky error pages, documents behind an expression of interest, iframes and ZIP files, a deadline in another timezone.

### 2. Supplier portal (Lieferantenportal, `customer-portal`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-customer-portal.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: The buyer's technical specification and its revisions.
- What makes it hard: Opens the oldest revision first, nested document viewers, paged requirement tables.

### 3. ERP (`erp`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-erp.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your company's materials, stock, lead times and price conditions with validity periods and quantity scales.
- What makes it hard: SAP-style transaction codes, an F4 search popup, status codes, a short session timeout.

### 4. Webmail (Werkpost, `mail`)

- URL: <https://atira-rfq-mail.kyora.run>
- Login: required; each run brings its own username and password in `access`
- Holds: Your sales inbox, with the sales director's discount approval and the signing TAN.
- What makes it hard: Look-alike approvals for other tenders, superseded approvals, an archive folder, paging.

## Public and private data

There are two datasets. The leaderboard uses the public one, on these websites. The final run uses a private dataset: the same jobs, bid rules and answer format, on different websites with other content and data. We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order: performance on the private dataset, performance on the public dataset, and the elegance of the system.

- **Public dataset:** The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too.
- **Private dataset (the final run):** When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

## Bid rules

The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.

1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.

## How a run works

Develop on your machine against the public websites with the scouting logins (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox: `atira test-run` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live, or drop the package on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). A test run lasts up to 2 hours on the public data and returns its score with the full breakdown. In the commands, `$ATIRA_TOKEN` holds your personal token (sign in with `atira login`, then `atira token`).

1. **Start.** The run issues a token, the task brief and fresh logins for every website.
2. **Read.** Your agent reads the brief, the rules and the answer format from the API.
3. **Work the websites.** It works through the 4 websites in a real browser and gathers the facts.
4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.
5. **Scored.** The answer is checked against the one correct answer; quality, cost and time are recorded.

### Develop locally

```sh
eval "$(atira scout --challenge rfq --env)"   # logins for the public websites
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting"   # the same, with the brief, as JSON
# run your agent on your machine, then once in the sandbox:
atira test-run ./my-agent --challenge rfq
```

`atira scout --env` exports the scouting logins as `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the shape a run gets), each website's URL, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the brief and the answer format. It also points the free hosted models at `atira models proxy` on your computer, so your agent needs no model key; another provider takes your own. Nothing done there counts. With these logins, an answer entered on the tender portal is acknowledged but never counts. In a run, your agent reads the same at `GET /v1/runs/current` with the run token as `x-api-key`, and hands in one valid answer of up to 65,536 bytes; a malformed one returns its problems while the clock keeps running.

### Read the run

Inside a test or scored run, with the run token (`$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`) in `RUN_TOKEN`:

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/runs/current" -H "x-api-key: $RUN_TOKEN"
```

The response holds `brief` (the task in Markdown, with the rules), `access` (each website's `url` and `credentials`), `submission` (where the answer goes), `answer_schema`, `expires_at`, `llm_proxy_url` and `llm_providers`. Outside a run, `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` returns the brief, logins, answer target and schema for the public websites, without a token.

### In the sandbox

A test run and a scored run start your `run` command with these variables. `setup` runs before, with network but without them, for up to 5 minutes that don't count toward your time.

| Variable | Value |
| --- | --- |
| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the platform API; the run is at /v1/runs/current |
| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | this run's token, sent as x-api-key |
| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON |
| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | the model proxy with the run token in its path; bring your own provider key |
| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | https://atira-challenge.kyora.run/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN/anthropic |
| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | https://atira-challenge.kyora.run/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN/openai/v1 |
| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | https://atira-challenge.kyora.run/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN/google |
| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL` | https://atira-challenge.kyora.run/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN/mistral |
| `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | https://atira-challenge.kyora.run/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN/together/v1 |
| `CLEF_BASE_URL`, `CLEF_API_KEY` | Clef through the proxy, https://atira-challenge.kyora.run/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN/clef, with the run token as its key; free, no usage cap. |
| `QWEN_BASE_URL`, `QWEN_API_KEY` | Qwen through the proxy, https://atira-challenge.kyora.run/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN/qwen/v1, with the run token as its key; free, no usage cap. |
| `CDP_URL` | the sandbox browser (Chrome DevTools Protocol), http://127.0.0.1:9222; with several, browser 1 |
| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: one per browser asked for in agent.json, up to 4 |
| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started, 1 to 4 |
| `DISPLAY` | the desktop browser 1 runs on, :1 at 1280×800; browser n is on :n |
| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY`, `http_proxy`, `https_proxy` | the only way out: the platform and the websites (http://127.0.0.1:3128) |
| `NO_PROXY`, `no_proxy` | reached directly, so the browser's CDP stays local (localhost,127.0.0.1) |
| `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY` | Node's fetch uses the proxy (1) |

Every model call goes through the platform's metering proxy, which records its tokens and cost; the hosted models need no key, and any other provider takes the team's own. [The run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls) has the key and SDK settings for each provider.

## Unlimited Inference

We host Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare's Clef for this hackathon, free and with no usage cap. On your laptop, `atira models proxy` gives you a URL and key (setup on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team#team-models)). In test and scored runs it's set up for you. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair.

### Qwen3.8-Flash-Next

#6 on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-8-flash-next) (open-weight, large models). Multimodal general-purpose LLM. Strong at reasoning, tool calls and reading pages and screenshots, with a 256k context, so it can plan, browse and write the answer.

- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 32 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
- **Simulated pricing:**
  - Input: $0.15 / M tokens
  - Cached input: $0.016 / M tokens
  - Cache writes: Free
  - Output: $0.47 / M tokens
- **Precision:** [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4) (NVIDIA's checkpoint)

Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.

```python
import os
from openai import OpenAI

qwen = OpenAI(
    base_url=os.environ["QWEN_BASE_URL"],
    api_key=os.environ["QWEN_API_KEY"],
)
reply = qwen.chat.completions.create(
    model="qwen",
    messages=[{
        "role": "user",
        "content": "Which button submits?",
    }],
)
```

### Cloudflare Clef

A multimodal decision model. Give it a state and up to 4 screenshots, then ask it questions: `choice` picks one of your options, `noul` gives the probability of yes, from 0 to 1, and `score` rates on a scale you set. See [Cloudflare's announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clef-decision-models/) and [the benchmarks](https://clef-evals.workers-ai-mle.workers.dev). Worth a try for quick, low-stakes decisions, such as which link to open or whether a page is the right document, while the bigger model reads and reasons.

- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 16 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
- **Simulated pricing:**
  - Input: $0.24 / M tokens
  - Output: Not priced

Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.

```sh
curl "$CLEF_BASE_URL/v1/decide" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLEF_API_KEY" \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
  "state": {"page": "Checkout returns 502"},
  "questions": {"next": {
    "type": "choice",
    "instructions": "What next?",
    "criteria": {
      "retry": "Retry the request",
      "report": "Report the error"}}}}'
```

In a run, `QWEN_BASE_URL` with `QWEN_API_KEY` and `CLEF_BASE_URL` with `CLEF_API_KEY` are set for you. On your machine, `atira models proxy` serves the same APIs on 127.0.0.1, so the same code works in both. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. An idle model can take several minutes to wake on its first call, so use long timeouts.

```sh
atira login   # once per computer
atira models proxy   # keep it running; it prints:
export QWEN_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/qwen/v1
export QWEN_API_KEY=local
export CLEF_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8765/clef
export CLEF_API_KEY=local
```

Cost and time count toward your rank, and a call to these models costs a fraction of a frontier call. Use them for the easy steps.

If one fails mid-run, retry the call, as with any provider. If they were down for most of a run that then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count, and a scored run starts again once by itself.

## Submitting

A submission is your agent as a gzipped tarball. It is reviewed automatically, then run once in the sandbox on the public dataset, and that score ranks your team. Submit as often as you like, one at a time; your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.

### agent.json

```json
{
  "setup": ["uv", "sync"],
  "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"],
  "models": ["qwen"]
}
```

Put `agent.json` at the root of the tarball, next to your code and its dependency file. Up to 20 MB compressed. `setup` installs dependencies with network access, within 5 minutes that don't count toward your time; `run` is timed and reaches only the platform and the websites. `"browsers": 1–4` (default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts, each on its own screen. `"models"` lists the hosted models your agent calls; the run waits only for those to warm up (for all of them when it's absent). Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, and Rust with cargo are installed. The [starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal skeleton to start from.

### Upload

```sh
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
  "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions"
```

Or drop the tarball on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team). Upload it as a test run first to watch it work in the sandbox: its browser live, its logs, and a recording afterwards.

### Test run first

The same tarball as a test run: one run in the scored-run sandbox on the public data, with live browser frames, logs and a recording.

```sh
tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" \
  -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
  "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals"
```

### Follow your submissions

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions" -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN"
```

Logs of test runs and scored runs, from a cursor (`after`); repeat with the returned `cursor` until `chunks` is empty:

```sh
curl "$ATIRA_API/v1/runs/$RUN_ID/logs?after=0" -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN"
```

## Scoring and ranking

Every submission is measured on its run in the sandbox.

- **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
- **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
- **Cost:** Every model call goes through the proxy and is priced per model. There is no budget: at equal quality, cost × time decides.
- **Time:** Wall-clock time from the start of the run until the answer is accepted. It weighs as much as cost: halving either halves cost × time.

Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.

Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.

## Fair play

Your agent has to find the answer itself.

- Your system must work the answer out from the websites at run time, with a model doing the navigating and deciding. A coding agent reviews every package; hardcoded answers, fixed scripts and crawlers are rejected.
- Bring your own model key for Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Together, Fireworks, kept as a team secret. Every call goes through the run's proxy and is metered at the published prices. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef are ours, unlimited. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair. The sandbox reaches the platform and the websites, nothing else.
- At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up to 4 in agent.json ("browsers"), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The sandbox stops any other browser your agent starts.
- One submission in flight per team. Submit again once it has finished.

Rules at a glance: [Fair play](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md)

"""
The model behind the workers: the hosted Qwen through the run's metering proxy by default.

AGENT_MODEL picks another model on the same OpenAI-compatible endpoint (QWEN_BASE_URL). Thinking is off for
navigation steps, which makes a step about three times faster, and on where a worker has to weigh evidence.
"""
import os
import time

import httpx2
from openai import AsyncOpenAI
from pydantic_ai.models.openai import OpenAIChatModel
from pydantic_ai.providers.openai import OpenAIProvider
from pydantic_ai.settings import ModelSettings

QWEN_MODEL = "qwen3.8-flash-next"
os.environ.setdefault("PYDANTIC_AI_NO_BANNER", "1")


async def _sent(request: httpx2.Request) -> None:
    request.extensions["sent_at"] = time.monotonic()


async def _answered(response: httpx2.Response) -> None:
    """Log each model call's status and seconds, so slow or hanging calls show in the run logs."""
    seconds = time.monotonic() - response.request.extensions.get("sent_at", time.monotonic())
    print(f"[model] {response.status_code} {seconds:.1f}s {len(response.request.content or b'')} bytes", flush=True)


def model() -> OpenAIChatModel:
    # The run waits for the hosted models to warm up, so a step answers in seconds; now and then a call hangs
    # until the proxy drops it minutes later, so give up early and retry instead.
    client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url=os.environ["QWEN_BASE_URL"], api_key=os.environ["QWEN_API_KEY"],
                         timeout=float(os.environ.get("LLM_TIMEOUT", "30")), max_retries=6,
                         http_client=httpx2.AsyncClient(event_hooks={"request": [_sent], "response": [_answered]}))
    return OpenAIChatModel(os.environ.get("AGENT_MODEL", QWEN_MODEL), provider=OpenAIProvider(openai_client=client))


def settings(thinking: bool = False) -> ModelSettings:
    return ModelSettings(
        temperature=0.2,
        parallel_tool_calls=False,  # one tab per worker: actions must run in order
        extra_body={"chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": thinking}},
    )
"""
The agent's entry point: agent.json runs `uv run --no-sync python agent.py`, in the sandbox and on your machine.

v1: read the brief, then sign and submit a bid with every position omitted (eligible, decision and reference
points). Workers for the specification, ERP and pricing come in v2+. See docs/plan.md.
"""
import asyncio
import json
import sys
import time

import browsers
import run as contract
from briefing import read_brief
from browser_tools import SiteSession
from playwright.async_api import async_playwright
from submit import Mailbox, submit_bid
from tracing import Trace

SAFETY_SECONDS = 90  # the answer must be in before the run expires
LOCAL_SECONDS = 20 * 60  # the scouting run does not expire; behave like a scored run


async def solve(task: dict, page) -> dict | None:
    """Enter the bid on the run's website (a "site" submission) and return None."""
    trace = Trace()
    left = min(contract.seconds_left(task), LOCAL_SECONDS)
    deadline = time.monotonic() + left - SAFETY_SECONDS
    briefing = await read_brief(task)
    trace.event("briefing", "done", **briefing.model_dump(exclude={"submission_steps"}))
    sites = {site["siteId"]: site for site in task["access"]}
    bid_context, mail_context = await browsers.more_contexts(page, 2)
    bid = SiteSession(sites[briefing.bid_site], bid_context, trace)
    mail = SiteSession(sites[briefing.mail_site], mail_context, trace)
    await asyncio.gather(bid.start(), mail.start())
    result = await submit_bid(bid, Mailbox(mail, briefing, deadline), briefing, deadline)
    trace.event("result", "done", result=result.model_dump() if result else None)
    return None


async def main() -> int:
    task, token = contract.load_run()
    sites = ", ".join(f"{site.get('siteId')} {site.get('url')}" for site in task["access"])
    print(f"Run {task.get('run_id') or '(local: the scouting logins, nothing counts)'}; websites: {sites}; "
          f"answer via {task['submission']['kind']}", flush=True)
    async with async_playwright() as playwright:
        browser, page = await browsers.connect(playwright)  # more browsers: browsers.connect(playwright, 1), ...
        answer = await solve(task, page)
    if answer is None:
        print("No answer to submit through the API: the bid is entered on the website", flush=True)
        return 0
    if not token:
        print("Your answer (locally nothing is submitted):", json.dumps(answer, ensure_ascii=False), flush=True)
        return 0
    status, body = contract.submit_answer(task, token, answer)
    print(f"Answer: HTTP {status} {body[:2000]}", flush=True)
    return 0 if status == 202 else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(asyncio.run(main()))

#!/bin/sh
# Run the agent locally against the public scouting sites (headless) and record it in experiments/local-runs.jsonl
# (gitignored). Usage, from anywhere: dev/run-local.sh <version> ["note"] [experiment]
# Needs `atira login` and `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. HEADLESS=0 shows the browser.
cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." || exit 1
version=${1:?usage: dev/run-local.sh <version> [note] [experiment]}
note=${2:-}
experiment=${3:-}
curl -s --max-time 5 -o /dev/null http://127.0.0.1:8765/ || {
  echo "The models proxy is not running: start \`atira models proxy\` in another terminal first."; exit 1; }
commit=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)
dirty=no; [ -n "$(git status --porcelain -- agent)" ] && dirty=yes
traces="$PWD/agent/traces/$(date -u +%Y%m%d-%H%M%S)"
mkdir -p "$traces"
eval "$(atira scout --env)"
(cd agent && uv sync -q && HEADLESS=${HEADLESS:-1} TRACE_DIR="$traces" uv run --no-sync python agent.py)
status=$?
trace=$(ls "$traces"/run-*.jsonl 2>/dev/null | head -1)
[ -n "$trace" ] || { echo "The agent wrote no trace; nothing recorded."; exit $status; }
python3 dev/track.py local --trace "$trace" --version "$version" --experiment "$experiment" --note "$note" \
  --commit "$commit" --dirty "$dirty" && python3 dev/track.py report
exit $status
---
# What we tried and learned

One bullet per experiment or failure: what changed, what happened, what we keep. Written by hand; run data is in
`experiments/runs.jsonl` (render it with `python3 dev/track.py report`).

- v0-starter test run: the starter kit's `solve()` stub exits without an answer; the sandbox scores that 0 and
  ineligible after 4 s.
- v1 local (first signed bid): the configurator worker needed 36 requests and 433 s for a bid with every position
  omitted; about 230 s of that went to the TAN round trips (153 s to 385 s).
- TAN loop: each TAN request invalidates the previous TAN, and the mail worker was started 6 times (2 hit the 8-request
  limit) before a fresh TAN reached the signing step in time. Fetch the TAN right after requesting it, in one sequence.
- Tokens: 247k input for a bid without positions, nearly all in the configurator worker; trim page views before v2.
- TAN lookup fixes: never put wall-clock time in a goal (the sites run on the scenario clock, so a TAN "requested at
  <today>" never shows up); "newest" is the highest request number. Short lookups run without note(), so the model
  returns its result instead of noting it and searching on.
- v1 first test run crashed at import: `llm.py` imported `httpx`, but openai 3.x depends on `httpx2`; the local venv
  still had a stale `httpx` from openai 2.x. Run `uv sync` after dependency changes so local matches the sandbox.
- v1 first scored test run: quality 10 (decision 5 + reference 5), eligible, 3.4 min, $0.022. Discount, total and
  total consistency score 0 even with every position omitted and total 0; positions need v2.
- v1 submission: review passed, quality 10, 4:41 min, $0.024; team rank #4. Submit from a clean `git archive` export
  of agent/ so unfinished files never reach the package reviewer.

"""The free hosted models in short: one call each. Docs: $API/start#models and $API/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls

Qwen (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next): an OpenAI-compatible chat model with tool calls, images and a 256k context. Every run gets
QWEN_BASE_URL and QWEN_API_KEY; on your machine `atira scout --env` points them at `atira models proxy`, which you
keep running in another terminal.

Clef (Cloudflare Clef): a decision model. POST $CLEF_BASE_URL/v1/decide with a `state`, up to 4 `images` and your
`questions`: "choice" picks one of your options, "noul" gives the probability of yes, "score" rates on your scale.
CLEF_BASE_URL and CLEF_API_KEY are set only where the platform hosts Clef. A run waits only for the models listed in
agent.json "models" to warm up: list ["qwen", "clef"] if your agent relies on Clef.

Any other provider works with your own key, through the run's metering proxy: see the docs above.
"""
import os

import httpx2 as httpx  # comes with the OpenAI SDK
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

QWEN_MODEL = "qwen3.8-flash-next"


def qwen() -> AsyncOpenAI:
    """A client for the hosted Qwen; a cold model takes a while to answer its first call, hence the long timeout."""
    return AsyncOpenAI(base_url=os.environ["QWEN_BASE_URL"], api_key=os.environ["QWEN_API_KEY"], timeout=360)


async def ask_qwen(prompt: str) -> str:
    """One chat call: the reply's text."""
    reply = await qwen().chat.completions.create(model=QWEN_MODEL, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}])
    return reply.choices[0].message.content or ""


async def ask_clef(state, question: str) -> float:
    """One decision: how likely Clef finds the answer to a yes/no question about `state` (text or JSON) is yes."""
    body = {"state": state, "questions": {"q": {"type": "noul", "instructions": question}}}
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=120) as client:
        response = await client.post(os.environ["CLEF_BASE_URL"].rstrip("/") + "/v1/decide", json=body,
                                     headers={"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['CLEF_API_KEY']}"})
    response.raise_for_status()
    return response.json()["answers"]["q"]["noul"]

# Atira starter kit

A minimal starting point, not an agent. It does the platform plumbing: it reads the run, attaches to the run's
browsers and shows how to call the free hosted models. Then it stops at `solve()` in `agent.py`, the place for your
agent. Out of the box it exits without an answer.

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `run.py` | The run contract: reads the run (`load_run`) and submits an API answer (`submit_answer`) |
| `browsers.py` | Attaches to the run's browsers over CDP and gets a page (`connect`); locally it starts a Chromium |
| `models.py` | One call to each hosted model: `ask_qwen` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) and `ask_clef` (Cloudflare Clef) |
| `agent.py` | The entry point: reads the run, connects browser 1, calls `solve(task, page)` and submits what it returns |
| `agent.json` | How the sandbox installs (`uv sync`, the versions in `uv.lock`) and runs it; it waits for the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The plumbing against fakes |

## Your agent goes in `solve()`

`solve(task, page)` gets the run and a Playwright page in browser 1:

- `task["brief"]`: the task and its rules;
- `task["access"]`: each website's `siteId`, `url` and `credentials`;
- `task["submission"]`: where the answer goes, `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` or `{"kind": "site", "url": ...}`;
- `task["answer_schema"]`: the JSON Schema of the answer.

For an `api` submission, return the answer and `main()` submits it: `202` is accepted and final, `400` lists the
issues to fix. For a `site` submission, enter the answer on that website yourself and return `None`. Reading pages,
acting on them and working out the answer are yours to build.

Mind the clock: a scored run has 20 minutes, and `run.seconds_left(task)` says how many seconds are left. Every part
of the answer scores on its own, so submit your best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
searching; an answer that comes too late scores 0.

More browsers: set `"browsers": 2` (up to 4) in `agent.json`, then `await browsers.connect(playwright, 1)` attaches
to browser 2.

## The hosted models in short

Both are free and need no key of yours: runs get the variables, and locally `atira scout --env` sets them, pointed
at `atira models proxy`.

```python
import models

text = await models.ask_qwen("Which button submits this form? ...")          # QWEN_BASE_URL, QWEN_API_KEY
yes = await models.ask_clef({"page": page_text}, "Is this the current revision?")  # CLEF_BASE_URL, CLEF_API_KEY
```

`models.qwen()` is an OpenAI SDK client, for tool calls, images and everything else. Clef is set only where the
platform hosts it; if your agent relies on it, list `"models": ["qwen", "clef"]` in `agent.json` so the run waits for
it to warm up. Another provider works with your own key through the run's metering proxy:
`$API/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls`.

## Run it locally

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) (open a new terminal after installing it, so
it is on your PATH) and the Atira CLI, signed in once with `atira login`.

Terminal 1: start the free models and leave it open.

```sh
atira models proxy
```

Terminal 2, in this folder:

```sh
uv sync && uv run playwright install chromium
eval "$(atira scout --env)"     # the scouting logins, and the model variables pointed at that proxy
uv run --no-sync python agent.py
```

In PowerShell on Windows, Terminal 2:

```powershell
uv sync; uv run playwright install chromium
atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression    # the same exports
uv run --no-sync python agent.py
```

A Chromium window opens (`HEADLESS=1` hides it). Nothing done with the scouting logins counts, and locally an answer
is printed, never submitted. If `atira` says `Unknown command: models`, run `atira upgrade`.

## Test-run it, then submit it

```sh
atira test-run .   # the sandbox, exactly like a scored run, on the public dataset; opens the run page live
atira submit .     # reviewed, then run once and scored for the leaderboard
```

Both pack this directory without what `.gitignore` excludes.

## Environment

| Variable | Set by | Used for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `CHALLENGE_API_URL`, `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | runs | the run, at `/v1/runs/current` |
| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING` | `atira scout --env` | locally: the brief and the scouting logins |
| `CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS` | runs | the sandbox's browsers; locally the kit starts its own Chromium |
| `QWEN_BASE_URL`, `QWEN_API_KEY` | runs, `atira scout --env` | the hosted Qwen |
| `CLEF_BASE_URL`, `CLEF_API_KEY` | runs, `atira scout --env`, when Clef is hosted | the hosted Clef |

## Docs

- How a run works: `$API/docs/run-contract.md`
- Building an agent: `$API/docs/building-an-agent.md`
- Fair play, the rules: `$API/docs/fair-play.md`

## Tests

```sh
uv run python -m unittest discover -s tests
```

# Atira Challenges

> Atira Challenges is a platform for agent hackathons in industrial sales. Teams build an agent system (one agent or several) that works through realistic business software, with any model through our proxy and their own tools. Each scored submission is reviewed automatically, run in an isolated sandbox on the public dataset, and ranked on a live leaderboard: eligible answers first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time. When the hackathon ends, every team's latest submission that passed review runs once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

The public pages are also Markdown: the home page, Getting started, each challenge, its leaderboard and each team's profile. Add `.md` to the URL (`/index.md` for the home page) or send `Accept: text/markdown`. For runs, use the API or the CLI's MCP tools. Everything works with plain HTTP, so `curl` and the API guide are enough. Send your personal token (`atira token` prints it after `atira login`; plain curl can use the device flow in the API guide) or the run token in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

If you are a team's coding agent: install the CLI (`curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh`, on Windows `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex`), have a team member run `atira login`, then add the CLI as your MCP server: `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Claude Code) or `codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Codex). Its tools start test runs (`test_run`), wait for them (`wait_for_run`), show why one failed (`diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_screenshot`, `run_inputs`) and submit (`submit`); [Debug runs from your coding agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md) lists them all. Run the agent locally against the public websites with `atira scout --env`, and start from the starter kit below. The agent you build must let a model choose where to go, what to search for and which documents matter, at run time: fixed scripts and crawlers that collect the websites for one model call are rejected in review, and so are values copied from the websites into the code.

Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too. When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

The [leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) shows the public dataset until the organizers publish the final results.

1689	
1690	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
1691	
1692	You build an agent system that does a real job on websites designed to be hard for agents. Eligible answers
1693	rank first, then by how right they are, then by LLM cost times run time: halving either counts the same. New here?
1694	`$API/start` walks you from sign-in to your first scored run, step by step.
1695	
1696	- **Sign in and form a team:** sign in with GitHub at `$API/team`, create your team (you become its captain) and
1697	  invite up to four teammates by their GitHub username (five people in all); each invite link works only for that
1698	  account. Your team page shows members, rank and history.
1699	- **Your terminal and your agent:** `curl -fsSL $API/install.sh | sh` (on Windows, in PowerShell:
1700	  `irm $API/install.ps1 | iex`) installs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md), with a private Node 24 if yours is missing, and
1701	  `atira login` signs it in through the browser. Each person gets their own token for each device, listed on the
1702	  team page under Signed-in devices, where you can revoke it; `atira token` prints it for curl and scripts.
1703	- **Everything in the browser:** your dashboard (`$API/team`) takes package uploads by drag and drop, lists every
1704	  run with a link to its live view, and keeps your team's secrets.
1705	- **Challenges:** each challenge is its own world with its own websites, task and answer format. The first one
1706	  is [RFQ](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md): turn a tender scattered across four German business websites into
1707	  one priced bid.
1708	- **Public and private data:** the websites and the scenario you scout and test-run on are the public dataset, and
1709	  every scored submission runs on it during the hackathon. The correct answer isn't published; your system has to
1710	  work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that
1711	  passed review once by default, or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts, on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the winners
1712	  ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from
1713	  the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
1714	- **Develop locally:** the scouting logins the organizers publish open the public websites to you and your agent.
1715	  `atira scout --env` exports them the way a run gets its logins, so your agent runs on your machine against the
1716	  real websites. Where the platform hosts models, they need no key there either: keep `atira models proxy` running
1717	  and `--env` points your agent at it; any other provider takes your own key. Nothing done with them counts. RFQ has one public
1718	  scenario, `public-1`.
1719	- **Sandbox test runs:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run and opens it live. It
1720	  runs once in exactly the sandbox scored runs use, against the public scenario: watch its browser, read its logs,
1721	  replay the recorded video, and get your score with the full breakdown. Use it to make sure your package works
1722	  before you submit; `atira cancel` stops a run early.
1723	- **Scored runs:** upload your agent system as a package. We review it, then run it once in the sandbox on the
1724	  public dataset and score it. Only these runs count for the leaderboard. Your best submission holds your place on
1725	  the leaderboard; your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.
1726	- **What wins:** eligible answers rank first, then answer quality; at equal quality, the lower LLM cost × wall-clock
1727	  time wins, each measured on the submission's scored run. The final run ranks the same way, choosing your single best attempt if you opted in to three. Each public submission runs
1728	  once.

1756	# The CLI
1757	
1758	A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins. It is made for
1759	people and coding agents alike: every command takes `--json`, and exit codes tell outcomes apart. Everything it does
1760	is plain HTTP, described in the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md); you never need the CLI.
1761	
1762	## Install
1763	
1764	macOS and Linux:
1765	
1766	```sh
1767	export ATIRA_API=https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai
1768	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | sh
1769	```
1770	
1771	Windows, in PowerShell (5.1 or 7):
1772	
1773	```powershell
1774	$env:ATIRA_API = "https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai"
1775	irm "$env:ATIRA_API/install.ps1" | iex
1776	```
1777	
1778	The script checks for Node 24 or newer. Where it is missing, it asks whether to install a private copy for atira
1779	alone, the latest Node 24 from nodejs.org, checked against the release's `SHASUMS256.txt`. It needs no admin rights
1780	and never changes the `node` on your `PATH`. Without a terminal to ask in, `ATIRA_INSTALL_NODE=1` says yes (`0`, no).
1781	Then it downloads `/cli.mjs`, checks it against `/cli.mjs.sha256` and installs it for you alone, without sudo:
1782	
1783	- macOS and Linux: the file in `~/.local/share/atira/atira.mjs`, Node (if needed) in `~/.local/share/atira/node`,
1784	  and an `atira` command in `~/.local/bin`. It tells you when `~/.local/bin` is not on your `PATH`.
1785	- Windows: the same under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira`, with `atira.cmd` in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\atira\bin`, which it adds to
1786	  your user `PATH`. Open a new terminal afterwards.
1787	
1788	The `atira` command runs your own Node when it is 24 or newer, else the private copy. Running the installer again
1789	updates the CLI; it downloads Node again only when the private copy is older than 24. Read the script first, if you
1790	like:
1791	
1792	```sh
1793	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/install.sh" | less
1794	```
1795	
1796	To uninstall: `rm -rf ~/.local/share/atira ~/.local/bin/atira`, or on Windows
1797	`Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:LOCALAPPDATA\atira"`. Your sign-in stays in the config file (see below) until you
1798	delete it.
1799	
1800	Without installing anything, download the file and run it with Node; `node atira.mjs` works wherever this guide
1801	says `atira`:
1802	
1803	```sh
1804	curl -fsSL "$ATIRA_API/cli.mjs" -o atira.mjs && node atira.mjs --help
1805	```
1806	
1807	The CLI talks to the server it was downloaded from. Set `ATIRA_API` to use another one. `atira upgrade` downloads the
1808	server's current version, checks its SHA-256 and replaces the file; a download that does not match leaves the file
1809	as it was.

1811	## Sign in
1812	
1813	```sh
1814	atira login
1815	```
1816	
1817	The browser opens a page that asks you to sign in with GitHub, then whether to sign in the CLI on this computer.
1818	Approve, and the browser returns to the CLI, which stores a personal token for you. The token acts as you, on the
1819	team you are in at the time of each request: leave the team, or be removed, and it no longer reaches the team. It
1820	lasts 90 days. Your team page lists your signed-in devices; revoke any of them there.
1821	
1822	Where no browser can open (an SSH session, a container, a coding agent), sign in with a code instead:
1823	
1824	```sh
1825	atira login --device
1826	```
1827	
1828	It prints a link with the code filled in. Open it on any device, check that the code matches and approve; the CLI
1829	waits and then stores the token. `atira login` switches to the code by itself when the browser cannot be opened, or
1830	offers it when the browser has not answered after two minutes.
1831	
1832	```sh
1833	atira whoami                                  # who you are, your team, and when the token expires
1834	atira token                                   # the token, for curl and scripts
1835	curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)" "$ATIRA_API/v1/teams/me"
1836	atira logout                                  # revoke the token on the server and forget it here
1837	```
1838	
1839	The token is kept per server in `~/.config/atira/config.json` (or `$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/atira/config.json`; on Windows
1840	`%USERPROFILE%\.config\atira\config.json`), readable only by you (mode 0600). `ATIRA_TOKEN` overrides it, which suits
1841	CI and agents: `export ATIRA_TOKEN=$(atira token)`.

1843	## Commands
1844	
1845	| Command | What it does |
1846	| --- | --- |
1847	| `login [--device] [--key <key>]` | Sign in through the browser, or with a code (`--device`), and store a personal token; `--key` stores a team key where there is no GitHub sign-in |
1848	| `logout` | Revoke the stored token on the server and forget it |
1849	| `whoami` | Who you are signed in as, your team, and when the token expires |
1850	| `token` | Print the token in use, for `curl -H "x-api-key: $(atira token)"` |
1851	| `upgrade` | Download the server's current CLI, check its SHA-256 and replace this file |
1852	| `challenges` | The challenges, with their Markdown pages |
1853	| `challenge <id>` | A challenge as Markdown: task, websites, rules, run contract, submitting, answer schema |
1854	| `scout [--challenge <id>] [--env [--port <port>]]` | The published scouting logins for the public websites; `--env` prints them as shell exports for running your agent locally, with any hosted model's variables pointed at `atira models proxy`; use the same `--port` when the proxy runs on another port |
1855	| `models proxy [--port <port>]` | Where the organizers host models: a local proxy to them on 127.0.0.1 (port 8765) that prints each model's base URL and key variables |
1856	| `test-run <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset and open its run page; `--follow` prints its place in the queue, then streams its logs here |
1857	| `submit <dir> [--challenge <id>] [--dry-run] [--follow] [--no-open]` | Pack a folder and submit it: review, then one scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page; `--follow` prints the review, each run's place in the queue and its end here |
1858	| `cancel <run>` | Cancel a test or scored run that has not finished: its sandbox is removed and the run fails |
1859	| `final [--best-of <1\|3>] [--challenge <id>]` | Read or change the final attempt choice before the final run starts |
1860	| `status [<id>] [--challenge <id>]` | Your latest submissions and test runs, or one submission (`sub_...`), test run (`reh_...`) or run (`run_...`) |
1861	| `logs <run> [--follow]` | A test or scored run's logs; `--follow` keeps polling until the run has ended |
1862	| `package <id> [--out <dir>]` | The package a test run (`reh_...` or `run_...`), scored run or submission (`sub_...`) of your team used, as uploaded: agent.json and each file's size; `--out` saves the `.tar.gz` in a folder, checked against its SHA-256 |
1863	| `leaderboard [--challenge <id>]` | The leaderboard |
1864	| `mcp` | Serve MCP on stdio for your coding agent: list and debug runs (why one failed, logs by time, model calls, where the time went, a browser's screen at a time, recorded inputs, two runs compared), start and wait for test runs, and cancel a run or submit when you confirm ([MCP guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md)) |
1865	
1866	Every command accepts `--json` (machine-readable output on stdout, errors included) and `--help`.
1867	`--challenge` defaults to `ATIRA_CHALLENGE`, else the platform's first challenge. While `login` waits, it writes its
1868	instructions to stderr, so `--json` output on stdout stays one JSON document.
1869	
1870	### Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
1871	
1872	Develop against the public websites on your own machine, then test the package in the sandbox:
1873	
1874	```sh
1875	atira scout                    # the scouting logins: each website, its URL, username and password
1876	eval "$(atira scout --env)"    # the same as shell exports
1877	uv run python agent.py         # your agent, on your machine, against the public websites (the starter kit's way)
1878	atira test-run ./my-agent      # then one run in the sandbox, opened live in the browser
1879	```
1880	
1881	On Windows, `--env` and `models proxy` print PowerShell's `$env:NAME = '...'` instead; load them with
1882	`atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`.
1883	
1884	### Hosted models from your machine
1885	
1886	Where the organizers host models, a run gets each one's base URL and key variables set for it, and the
1887	Getting started page names them. On your machine, run the proxy in its own terminal: it prints the same variables,
1888	pointed at itself, with `local` as the key (any non-empty value works through it).
1889	
1890	```sh
1891	atira login                    # once per computer
1892	atira models proxy             # keep it running; it prints the exports
1893	```
1894	
1895	`eval "$(atira scout --env)"` sets the same variables with the scouting logins; it never exports your sign-in. The proxy
1896	listens on 127.0.0.1 only. It holds a 30-minute inference token, good for model calls only and bound to an Ed25519 key
1897	that never leaves the process, signs every call with that key and rotates the token before it expires. A copied token
1898	works in no other client. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. If port 8765 is in use, pick
1899	the same port for the proxy and the scouting exports:
1900	
1901	```sh
1902	atira models proxy --port 8777                   # in a second terminal
1903	eval "$(atira scout --env --port 8777)"
1904	```
1905	
1906	In PowerShell, the second line is `atira scout --env --port 8777 | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`. The proxy also
1907	prints the command with its actual port, including when `--port 0` lets the operating system choose one.
1908	
1909	`scout` needs no sign-in for the logins. It prints the logins the organizers published, how long they are valid,
1910	and what happens to an answer: these are demo logins, so an answer entered on the website that takes it is
1911	acknowledged without counting. For RFQ, a bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting. `--json` prints what
1912	`GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returns: the logins as `access`, plus `submission`, `brief` and `answer_schema`,
1913	shaped like a run's `/v1/runs/current`. `--env` prints:
1914	
1915	| Variable | Value |
1916	| --- | --- |
1917	| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING` | what `GET /v1/challenges/<id>/scouting` returned, as JSON: the brief, logins and answer format |
1918	| `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` | `$ATIRA_API/v1/challenges/<id>/scouting`, the same without a token once the organizers publish the logins |
1919	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with the scouting logins, the JSON a run gets: `[{"siteId", "url", "credentials": {"username", "password"}}]` |
1920	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL` | each website's URL, its id upper-cased with `_` for other characters, e.g. `CHALLENGE_SITE_TENDER_PORTAL_URL` |
1921	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | only when the platform hosts models: each one through `atira models proxy` on this computer, with `local` as the key. Keep the proxy running in another terminal, signed in with `atira login`. `atira scout --help` names them |
1922	
1923	With `--env --json`, the same variables come as one JSON object. There is no run token: your agent calls other
1924	models with your own key, directly or through the model proxy with your personal token (see
1925	[LLM calls](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)). Calls through the proxy from your machine, a hosted model's included, are
1926	recorded for your team and never ranked. A hosted model is free to use, never charged; each call counts toward your
1927	run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest. Nothing done with these logins counts.
1928	Locally there are no browsers from the platform (`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `DISPLAY`) and no egress
1929	proxy: your agent starts its own browsers. When nothing is published yet, `scout` exits 4: organizers publish the scouting logins before the event.

1931	### Test runs and submissions
1932	
1933	```sh
1934	atira test-run ./my-agent --dry-run   # what would be uploaded, and what is left out
1935	atira test-run ./my-agent             # one run in the sandbox on the public dataset; opens its run page
1936	atira test-run ./my-agent --follow    # the same, and its logs here until it ends
1937	atira cancel run_...                  # stop a run that has not finished
1938	atira submit ./my-agent               # review, then the scored run on the public dataset; opens your team page
1939	atira status sub_...
1940	```
1941	
1942	`test-run` uploads the package, starts the test run and, when its output goes to a terminal, opens the run page in
1943	the browser: the browser, the logs, the phases and the score with its full breakdown, live. `submit` opens your team
1944	page instead, which shows the submission's review and then links each scored run as it starts: the run does not
1945	exist until the review has passed, which takes minutes, so the CLI does not wait for it unless you pass `--follow`.
1946	`ATIRA_BROWSER` picks the
1947	command that opens the page (`none` only prints the link), `--no-open` skips it, and `--json` never opens anything.
1948	
1949	`test-run --follow` then streams the run's logs as `logs --follow` does and exits 7 if the run failed or timed out.
1950	While the run waits for a sandbox, it prints its place in the [fair queue](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#the-run-queue) on stderr whenever
1951	that changes ("Queued: 3 runs ahead of yours"). With `--json --follow`, the upload's result comes as one JSON line,
1952	then one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` line per chunk. `submit --follow` prints the review's outcome, then each scored
1953	run's place in the queue and its end, and exits 7 unless the submission completes; with `--json`, the final
1954	submission follows the upload's line.
1955	
1956	`cancel <run>` takes a run (`run_...`) or a test run (`reh_...`) of your team that has not finished. The run's sandbox
1957	is removed and the run fails with the error "Cancelled by @you"; a queued run is cancelled before it starts. Your
1958	team can start the next test run at once. A cancelled scored run leaves its submission not complete: the leaderboard
1959	ignores that submission, and you can submit again. A run that
1960	has already finished answers 409 (exit 6).
1961	
1962	`test-run` and `submit` pack the folder into a gzipped tarball the way the platform reads it:
1963	
1964	- `agent.json` must be at the folder's root, with `run` (and optionally `setup`) as arrays of strings.
1965	- `.git`, `node_modules` and `.DS_Store` are always left out, and so is whatever `.gitignore` files exclude (in the
1966	  folder and below: patterns, `*`, `?`, `**`, `[...]`, a leading `/`, a trailing `/` for folders, and `!` to
1967	  include again). Symbolic links are left out too.
1968	- The limits are checked before uploading: at most 2,000 files, 5 MB per file, 20 MB in total, and 20 MB
1969	  compressed (or what the server announces).

1971	### Logs, status and the leaderboard
1972	
1973	`package <id>` shows exactly what a run ran: the package's SHA-256 and label, its `agent.json` and every file with
1974	its size. A scored run ran its submission's package. `--out ./downloaded` also saves the `.tar.gz` there; unpack it
1975	with `tar -xzf <file> -C <folder>`.
1976	
1977	`logs <run>` prints what the run has written so far; `--follow` polls with a growing pause (1 s, up to 10 s) and
1978	exits when the run has ended. `--json` prints one `{"at", "stream", "text"}` object per line. `status` without an id
1979	shows your best result, your latest submissions and your latest test runs.

2019	# Answers and scoring
2020	
2021	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
2022	
2023	Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
2024	ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
2025	websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
2026	isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
2027	on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).
2028	
2029	## Per run
2030	
2031	- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
2032	- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
2033	  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
2034	- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
2035	- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.
2036	
2037	A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
2038	is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.
2039	
2040	## Leaderboard
2041	
2042	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
2043	keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
2044	complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
2045	the run's own value.
2046	
2047	1. Eligible before ineligible.
2048	2. Higher quality.
2049	3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
2050	   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
2051	   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
2052	4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.
2053	
2054	On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
2055	the teams no other eligible team beats on both.
2056	
2057	Test runs and scored runs on the public scenario `public-1` show your team the points for each part of the answer,
2058	never the expected values. Runs on the private dataset show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.
2059	
2060	## Final run
2061	
2062	When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
2063	answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
2064	
2065	## Winners
2066	
2067	We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:
2068	
2069	1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
2070	2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
2071	3. The elegance of the system.
2072	
2073	It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
2074	latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
2075	publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
2076	public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
2077	`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).
2078	
2079	## RFQ scoring
2080	
2081	The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
2082	`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
2083	ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
2084	project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
2085	The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
2086	omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.
2087	
2088	| Part (a bid) | Points |
2089	| --- | --- |
2090	| Decision | 5 |
2091	| Tender reference | 5 |
2092	| Discount percent | 5 |
2093	| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
2094	| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
2095	| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
2096	| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
2097	| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |
2098	
2099	
2100	For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
2101	points but leaves the other fields their credit.
2102	
2103	Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
2104	one position's share each.
2105	
2106	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
2107	
2108	The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
2109	Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
2110	`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
2111	When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
2112	Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
2113	counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
2114	It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
2115	Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
2116	Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
2117	on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.
2118	
2119	Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
2120	the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
2121	rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.
